Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Religious Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The naming of a child in African Traditional Religion carries a lot of significance. Discuss

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In African Traditional Religion, the naming of a child is a major rite of passage, which follows birth and incorporates the child into the family, the community and the spiritual world. A name is never just a label: it expresses belief, history and hopes. The details vary among peoples, but the main significance can be set out as follows.

**1. It gives the child an identity.** The name distinguishes the child as a person and as a member of a particular family and clan. Without a name a child is not fully recognised as a member of the community, and in some societies the child is named only after a number of days (often in the first weeks), when it seems likely to survive.

**2. It integrates the child into the community.** The naming ceremony is public: relatives, neighbours and elders gather, bless the child and share in a feast. The community promises to care for the child and the child is introduced to the group, so the ceremony strengthens kinship and social bonds.

**3. It has religious meaning.** Prayers, libations and sometimes sacrifices are offered to God, the divinities and the ancestors, thanking them for the safe delivery of the child and asking for protection, health and long life. Water or other symbolic materials may be used, and the elders pronounce the name before the ancestors, which places the child under their protection.

**4. It may express the belief in reincarnation or the return of ancestors.** Among several peoples a child may be named after a deceased relative, because the child is believed to be that relative returning. Yoruba names such as Babatunde ("father has returned") or Yetunde ("mother has returned") are well-known examples. This links the child with the ancestors and the living with the dead.

**5. It records circumstances of birth.** Names may refer to the day of the week of birth (among the Akan, Kofi for a boy born on Friday and Kwame for a boy born on Saturday), the order of birth, twins, the season or events at the time of birth (famine, war, a visitor's arrival). This gives the name historical and social meaning.

**6. It expresses a belief about destiny and the child's character.** A name may predict or invoke the future of the child, such as wealth, wisdom, long life or leadership. Many people believe that a name influences the destiny and character of its bearer, and that is why elders choose names with care, sometimes after consulting a diviner.

**7. It praises or refers to God.** Many names include a name of God or a divinity (for example "God has given", "God's gift", "the Lord is great"), so that the child's name is a continuous reminder and a confession of faith.

**8. It transmits cultural values and history.** Names carry proverbs, family history, hopes and warnings, and so they pass on the language, the traditions and the memory of the people from one generation to the next.

**9. It involves taboos and protection.** Some peoples give "protective names" (for example names showing a child is unwanted or worthless) to deceive evil spirits when previous children have died. Names may also be kept secret or not used by strangers for fear of misuse.

**Discussion.** Today many Africans bear Christian or Muslim names, and naming ceremonies are mixed with baptism or Islamic naming rites. Yet traditional names and ceremonies continue, which proves their lasting significance.

**Conclusion.** The naming of a child carries religious, social, cultural and psychological significance: it integrates the child into the family and the community, places the child under spiritual protection, links the living with the ancestors and expresses beliefs about destiny. For this reason it is treated as a sacred event.
